svg.title: uRPF modes, the topologies each one breaks in, and the silent way it fails
svg.desc: Left: three modes. Strict mode checks that the source address is reachable through the interface the packet arrived on, which is correct on a single-homed edge and wrong everywhere traffic is asymmetric. Loose mode checks only that the source is reachable somewhere in the routing table, which stops random spoofing but not spoofing of an address inside your own space. Feasible-path or VRF mode checks against a specific table, which is the answer for an MPLS or VRF environment but only if the table is populated correctly. Right: the asymmetric scenario - a site has two providers, the outbound path uses provider A and the return path provider B, so strict mode drops the return traffic because the source is not reachable through B. The symptom is a one-way call, an intermittent failure, or a service that works from one branch and not another, and the drop counter is in show ip traffic rather than in any interface counter anyone looks at. Bottom: the decision rule - strict where single-homed, loose where multihomed, and never enable it on a link you have not traced in both directions. A footer notes that uRPF is a spoofing control, not an authorization control: it does nothing about a host using its own legitimate address.
svg.text: uRPF is a topology check wearing the clothes of a security control
It fails silently, one direction at a time, and the counter is not on the interface page anyone opens.

Decision rule: strict where single-homed, loose where multihomed, feasible-path only inside a VRF design - and never on a link whose return path you have not traced.
And keep the scope honest: uRPF stops source spoofing. It does nothing about a compromised host using its own legitimate address, which is the more common starting point.
Where the topology is too messy, the alternative is a source-based ACL or IP source guard at the access layer, not a weaker uRPF mode everywhere.
